Data Session 12, part 2: Building a Score From Scratch

84-355 Democracy’s Data | The Supreme Court’s votes, 1946–2023

Jonathan Cervas

August 09, 2026

  • Where did that number come from?
  • Part 1 — What one row is

Everything here runs as given. Your job is to read what comes out and say what it means.

Where did that number come from?

“The most conservative Court since the 1930s.”

This morning you used DW-NOMINATE: a number that places each member of Congress on a left–right line, computed from roll calls. You took the number as given.

Today you build one.

The Supreme Court is the easiest place to do it. Nine people, every vote recorded, every case public, and a database going back to 1946 that has counted all of it. And unlike Congress, the number of people is small enough that you can see the whole thing at once.

There are published scores for the Court — Martin-Quinn is the standard one. We are not using them, for a reason worth stating: a published score is the answer, and this session is about how the answer gets made.

Part 1 — What one row is

ag <- read.csv("data/agreement.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
jj <- read.csv("data/justices.csv",  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

nrow(jj)
#> [1] 10
jj
#>        justice cases pct_conservative pct_in_majority
#> 1    ACBarrett   222             61.3            90.9
#> 2  BMKavanaugh   234             60.3            95.5
#> 3      CThomas   232             67.7            79.3
#> 4       EKagan   234             33.8            74.0
#> 5    JGRoberts   234             59.8            94.3
#> 6    KBJackson   110             33.6            78.3
#> 7    NMGorsuch   232             57.8            81.3
#> 8      SAAlito   230             70.0            82.0
#> 9     SGBreyer   122             38.5            72.1
#> 10  SSotomayor   234             32.1            70.7

Ten justices sat between the 2020 and 2023 terms. For each we have how many cases they voted in, what share of their votes the database codes as conservative, and how often they were in the majority.

Note that Breyer and Jackson have about half as many cases as the others — Breyer retired during the window and Jackson replaced him. That will matter in Part 4.

Part 2 — Who agrees with whom

The raw material for any ideal-point score is embarrassingly simple: how often does each pair of people vote the same way?

head(ag[order(-ag$pct), c("a", "b", "pct", "cases")], 5)
#>              a           b  pct cases
#> 12 BMKavanaugh   JGRoberts 96.2   234
#> 30      EKagan  SSotomayor 92.3   234
#> 39   KBJackson  SSotomayor 90.9   110
#> 29      EKagan    SGBreyer 90.2   122
#> 1    ACBarrett BMKavanaugh 89.6   222
head(ag[order( ag$pct), c("a", "b", "pct", "cases")], 5)
#>          a          b  pct cases
#> 24 CThomas SSotomayor 53.0   232
#> 44 SAAlito SSotomayor 53.5   230
#> 23 CThomas   SGBreyer 53.7   121
#> 43 SAAlito   SGBreyer 55.0   120
#> 28  EKagan    SAAlito 55.7   230

Kavanaugh and Roberts agreed 96.2% of the time. Kagan and Sotomayor, 92.3%. At the other end, Thomas and Sotomayor agreed 53.0% — barely better than a coin.

That is the whole dataset. Forty-five numbers, one per pair. No ideology has been supplied to it. Nobody has told this table who is liberal.

Except one of the forty-five is not a number at all:

ag[ag$cases == 0, ]
#>            a        b agree cases pct
#> 38 KBJackson SGBreyer     0     0  NA

Breyer and Jackson never sat on a case together — she replaced him. Their agreement is not low or high; it is undefined, and no amount of data will fix it. Hold that thought for thirty seconds.

Part 3 — The score falls out

Now the move that makes DW-NOMINATE, Martin-Quinn, and every other ideal-point score work. Take the agreement rates as a measure of closeness, treat disagreement as distance, and ask: if these ten people had to be arranged along a single line so that people who agree sit near each other, what line would that be?

js <- sort(unique(c(ag$a, ag$b)))
M <- matrix(NA_real_, length(js), length(js), dimnames = list(js, js))
diag(M) <- 1
for (i in seq_len(nrow(ag))) {
  if (ag$cases[i] == 0) next          # Breyer and Jackson: no shared cases
  r <- ag$agree[i] / ag$cases[i]
  M[ag$a[i], ag$b[i]] <- r
  M[ag$b[i], ag$a[i]] <- r
}

# The scaling cannot take a hole. We fill the one missing pair with the average
# agreement across every other pair -- which is a GUESS, and the most
# conservative one available: it assumes nothing about whether they would have
# agreed. Part 6 Option B asks what happens if you refuse to guess.
M[is.na(M)] <- mean(M[upper.tri(M)], na.rm = TRUE)

score <- cmdscale(as.dist(1 - M), k = 1)[, 1]
round(sort(score), 3)
#>     CThomas     SAAlito   NMGorsuch   ACBarrett   JGRoberts BMKavanaugh 
#>      -0.218      -0.217      -0.132      -0.120      -0.074      -0.073 
#>   KBJackson      EKagan    SGBreyer  SSotomayor 
#>       0.151       0.206       0.231       0.246

That fill is a modeling decision, made by us, in one line. Option B has you remove it, and when you do, two adjacent pairs swap places — Thomas and Alito, and Roberts and Kavanaugh. Published scores make dozens of choices like this one. The difference is that ours is visible and reversible.

o <- sort(score)
plot(o, rep(0, length(o)), pch = 19, cex = 1.6, col = "#2c7fb8",
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "position recovered from agreement alone",
     ylim = c(-1, 1), xlim = range(o) * 1.25)
text(o, 0.25, names(o), srt = 45, adj = 0, cex = 0.75)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey70")

Read the order. Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Barrett, Roberts, Kavanaugh — then a gap — then Jackson, Kagan, Breyer, Sotomayor.

That is the ideological ordering of the Roberts Court as every court reporter in America would give it. It came out of forty-five agreement rates. We never told the model that Thomas is conservative, that these are political questions, or even that the people are judges.

jj$score <- score[jj$justice]
round(cor(jj$score, jj$pct_conservative), 3)
#> [1] -0.975

Correlation −0.975 with each justice’s share of conservative votes — a variable the scaling never saw. That is what an ideal-point score is: a summary of agreement that turns out to line up with something we already had a word for.

And notice the gap. The six on the left span 0.145. The distance from Kavanaugh to Jackson is 0.224, larger than the entire conservative bloc. This is not a spectrum with people spread along it. It is two clusters.

Part 4 — The number that surprises people more

jj[order(-jj$pct_in_majority), c("justice", "pct_conservative", "pct_in_majority")]
#>        justice pct_conservative pct_in_majority
#> 2  BMKavanaugh             60.3            95.5
#> 5    JGRoberts             59.8            94.3
#> 1    ACBarrett             61.3            90.9
#> 8      SAAlito             70.0            82.0
#> 7    NMGorsuch             57.8            81.3
#> 3      CThomas             67.7            79.3
#> 6    KBJackson             33.6            78.3
#> 4       EKagan             33.8            74.0
#> 9     SGBreyer             38.5            72.1
#> 10  SSotomayor             32.1            70.7
plot(jj$score, jj$pct_in_majority, pch = 19, col = "#C41230", cex = 1.3,
     xlab = "position (left = conservative here)", ylab = "% of the time in the majority")
text(jj$score, jj$pct_in_majority, jj$justice, pos = 3, cex = 0.65)

Kavanaugh is in the majority 95.5% of the time. Roberts, 94.3%. The lowest are Sotomayor at 70.7% and Breyer at 72.1% — and, on the other side, Thomas at 79.3%.

The two justices nearest the middle of that line win almost every case. The justices at either end lose most often. “Moderate” here is not a description of anyone’s opinions — it is a description of how often you are on the winning side, and it is a mechanical consequence of where you sit.

Part 5 — Seventy-eight terms

bt <- read.csv("data/by_term.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
c(terms = nrow(bt), from = min(bt$term), to = max(bt$term))
#> terms  from    to 
#>    78  1946  2023
plot(bt$term, bt$pct_conservative, type = "l", col = "grey60",
     xlab = "term", ylab = "% of decisions coded conservative")
lines(bt$term, filter(bt$pct_conservative, rep(1/5, 5), sides = 2),
      col = "#C41230", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 50, lty = 3)

The same database goes back to 1946, so the long series is free. The red line is a five-term moving average.

Before believing any story you see in it, notice what is being plotted: the share of decisions the database’s coders labelled conservative. That is a human judgement, applied case by case, for seventy-eight years, by people following a codebook. It is a good codebook. It is still a judgement, and it is the thing the whole series is made of.

Part 6 — Your turn

Change one thing, re-run, and write about what changed. Pick one.

Option A — Two dimensions. Change k = 1 to k = 2 in the scaling and plot both. Does the second dimension separate anybody the first one merged? If it does, what might it be picking up — and how would you tell that from noise?

Option B — Refuse to guess. Part 3 filled the Breyer–Jackson hole with the average. Instead, drop both of them from ag and re-run the scaling on the eight justices who overlap completely. Does the order of those eight change? What does the comparison tell you about how much the fill was doing?

Option C — The close cases. close_cases.csv has the 30 one-vote decisions in this window and who was in the majority for each. Count how often each justice was in the majority in those cases only, and compare to Part 4. Does the middle still win when it is close?

Option D — Your own question. 45 pairs, 10 justices, 78 terms.

What this lab cannot tell you

  • Whether “conservative” means the same thing across seventy-eight years. The codebook is consistent; the politics are not. A 1962 case coded conservative and a 2022 one may have almost nothing in common.
  • Why anyone voted as they did. Agreement is not agreement about reasons. Two justices can reach the same result from incompatible doctrines, and this data cannot see the difference — which is most of what law professors argue about.
  • That the line is real. We chose one dimension and it fit well. That does not prove judicial disagreement is one-dimensional; it proves a single dimension explains much of the variation in these votes, in this window.
  • What Martin-Quinn would say. The published scores use a more careful model that lets positions move over time. Ours is a snapshot, and it cannot show anyone changing.

On the discussion board

By Friday, 11:59 p.m. A sentence or two is enough.

Three that would make good posts:

  • We recovered the standard left–right ordering of the Court without ever mentioning ideology. Is that impressive, or is it circular?
  • The two justices in the middle win 95% of cases and the ones at the ends lose a third of them. Should that bother anybody?
  • Every number in Part 5 depends on a coder deciding what “conservative” means. Does that make the series useless, or just human?

Where the data came from

The Supreme Court Database, Washington University in St. Louis, 2024 release 01, justice-centered by citation — every justice’s vote in every case since 1946. http://scdb.wustl.edu/data.php

Note the protocol: the site serves over http only, and https fails.

Agreement and scaling use the 2020–2023 terms, and cases where the database records no ideological direction are excluded, because “voted the same way” is undefined without a direction to compare. The build is in data/build-data.R.
